qs.q: A 57-year-old woman has experienced episodes of altered mental status for the past month. On physical examination, she has bilateral carotid artery bruits. She is given folic acid supplementation. Which of the following laboratory test findings is she most likely to have?
qs.e: An elevated plasma homocysteine level is a risk for atherosclerosis as well as thrombosis. Her findings point to transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) with risk for stroke. The carotid bruits represent arterial narrowing as the result of atherosclerosis.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The carotid arteries supply the brain and face; they are key landmarks for vascular and neurological assessment. Understanding their course, branches, and relations helps diagnose stroke, carotid disease, and manage neck trauma.

sections.p: The carotid system consists of the common carotid arteries, which bifurcate into internal and external branches. They are the main suppliers of blood to the head and neck.
b: Bifurcation at the level of the fourth cervical vertebra

sections.p: Each common carotid artery rises from the aortic arch (left) or brachiocephalic trunk (right), travels up the neck, and divides into internal and external carotid arteries.
b: Internal carotid enters the skull via carotid canal; external gives off facial, lingual, occipital, etc. branches

sections.p: The carotid arteries lie in the carotid sheath, surrounded by the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve. The internal carotid is medial to the external carotid.
b: Facial nerve (CN VII) runs in the sheath; carotid bifurcation is a landmark for carotid endarterectomy

sections.p: The internal carotid supplies the anterior circulation of the brain, while the external carotid supplies the face and scalp.
b: Internal carotid gives ophthalmic, middle cerebral, anterior cerebral branches

sections.p: The carotid sinus is innervated by glossopharyngeal (CN IX) afferents, modulating heart rate and blood pressure.
They deliver oxygenated blood to the brain and regulate cerebral perfusion. The carotid sinus monitors blood pressure.
Carotid disease (stenosis, plaque) leads to stroke; trauma can cause pseudoaneurysm or dissection. Palpation of the carotid pulse aids in assessing hemodynamics.

t.b: Assesses plaque burden and flow velocity; high peak systolic velocity suggests significant stenosis.
Visualizes vessel lumen and plaque morphology; useful when surgery is considered.
Tests baroreceptor sensitivity; a positive response indicates intact reflex.

sections.p: Remember the carotid bifurcation is a key surgical landmark. A carotid bruit is often heard in atherosclerotic disease. In trauma, look for Horner’s syndrome as a sign of sympathetic chain injury.
b: Bifurcation at C4; external carotid gives facial nerve branches

sections.p: Treat underlying atherosclerosis with antiplatelet therapy and statins; manage hypertension. In symptomatic stenosis, consider endarterectomy or stenting.
The subclavian artery can be mistaken for the carotid in imaging; the vertebral artery supplies posterior circulation.
b: Subclavian vs carotid: different origins and territories

sections.p: A normal carotid duplex in a patient with atherosclerosis may occur if plaque is non-flow limiting; clinical assessment remains essential.
b: Low peak systolic velocity does not rule out significant plaque

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden unilateral weakness or speech difficulty (possible stroke), severe neck pain after trauma, sudden vision loss (carotid ophthalmic branch compromise)

faq.a: A whooshing sound heard over the carotid artery, indicating turbulent flow due to plaque or stenosis.

faq.q: Why is the carotid sinus important?
faq.a: It senses blood pressure changes and triggers reflexes that regulate heart rate and vascular tone.
